High-dimensional Schrödinger equations are a key component in a variety of fields including physics, biology, and chemistry. However, due to the curse of dimensionality, solving these equations is extremely challenging, especially when using traditional finite difference methods which results in computationally infeasible costs. To address this issue, a novel approach has been developed which employs a neural network to approximate the solution, thereby circumventing the curse of dimensionality in theory. Yet, this approach suffers from a fundamental flaw at the basis of its functionality where it incorrectly generalizes the network's output for out-of-range input combinations. Consequently, this leads to inaccurate estimates in the adjoint equation which hampers the efficiency of the adjoint-based optimization used in this method. To rectify this issue, two distinct solutions have been proposed which either utilize an expanded input space to maintain consistency or an adjusted neural network output to generate solutions. The efficacy of these solutions has been validated through numerical experiments which demonstrate the improved accuracy and efficiency of the neural network-based approach for high-dimensional Schrödinger equations.

In comprehension challenges like the C. Elegans Behavioral Quantification task, understanding neural processes is vital to bypassing issues in series prediction. A major hurdle is accurately mimicking neural activity dynamics, often solved with temporal models. We developed a method to create a temporal network that can learn and simulate neuronal connections, recreating neuronal behavior. Unlike existing approaches using MDP temporal frameworks, our model directly translates to a regression problem, simplifying training and output forecasting. We compared our approach with alternative methods using actual C. Elegans brain data, demonstrating more accurate predictions for motor neuron behavior and overall locomotion. We also assessed the ability of our model to detect changes in parameters, such as cholinergic activity in motor neurons. Our work provides a new method for tackling neuroscience problems involving neural activity simulation, offering a practical solution over more complex temporal frameworks. The code is available on https://github.com/amberthery/CAS-MRNN.

The equilibrium phase map of the stationary vertex woodlands model exhibits a phase transition as temperature decreases, transforming from a continuous spin glass phase to an ordered polar phase through a first-order transition. Within the spin glass phase, a twisted and fragmented phase emerges. This study explores the conditions that limit the occurrence of these phases within specific regions of parameter space. It demonstrates that the spin glass phase is confined to certain temperature and parameter ranges, resulting in the appearance of the polar and twisted phases through a series of bifurcations. Moreover, it highlights that the polar phase emerges through a first-order transition that begins with a saddle-node bifurcation outside this region. Ultimately, it reveals that additional twisted phases can arise through a similar type of bifurcation, but only if the associated saddle-node bifurcation occurs within a more restricted set of parameters.

A robust Gelfand pair for SL(2,p) is defined as a pair (H,ρ) consisting of a subgroup H of SL(2,p) and a irreducible representation ρ, such that the subgroup's orbits on the space ρ are robustly distinct. In the case of SL(2,p), the condition is equivalent to the group's 1-normality in ρ. It is known that 1-normality is equivalent to weak normality for irreducible characters of SL(2,p). A robust Gelfand pair for SL(2,p) can be seen as a robust Gelfand pair for PSp(2,p), considering the quotient group [SL(2,p),ρ] / {±1}.

This research examines the molecular pentaquarks with the strangeness of -3, which have an I = 1/2 I = 3/2 isospin structure and are comprised of concealed-charm components, using the quark model. Two possible structures for these molecules are considered, which have different diquark and antidiquark combinations in the presence of a strangeness quark. Utilizing the methods of Regge expansion and spin-flavor symmetry, the authors calculate the electromagnetic form factors for these pentaquark systems. In addition, the relativistic light-cone quantization approach is used to calculate their transition form factors and decay widths for the electromagnetic decay of the molecular pentaquarks to the J / psi and eta prime mesons. Our calculations also predict the magnitude of their anomalous magnetic moments. Notably, the results demonstrate that the anomalous magnetic moment is distinct for the two-potential models of the molecular pentaquarks. This research may guide the experimental discovery of the pentaquarks, which has the strangeness of -3 and is part of the P_{c}(4315) family discovered in 2015.

This paper examines properties of $n$-ary Zinbiel algebras, focusing on their finite dimensionality and characteristic. It is shown that if a $n$-ary algebra $A$ of characteristic $p>3$ includes a non-zero element $a \in A$ such that $T_{p-1}(a)=0$, where $T_{p-1}(a)$ represents the $p-1$-th Zinbiel coefficient of $a$, which is zero. The paper establishes that if an $n$-ary algebra $A$ meets this condition, its commutator ideal $A'$ generated by the commutators of its elements is a nilpotent ideal and the quotient algebra $A/A'$ is a commutative $n$-ary hyperassociative algebra. It also proves that if an $n$-ary algebra $A$ has a characteristic $p>3$ and includes a non-zero element $a \in A$ such that $T_{p-1}(a)=0$, its commutator subalgebra $A'$ will be a nilpotent subalgebra and the quotient algebra $A/A'$ will be a commutative $n$-ary hyperautomative algebra.

This paper explores the scattering theory for a time-dependent equation that incorporates both random movement and a specific potential in three-dimensional space: $iu_t + \Delta u - \frac{1}{2}u^2Q(x) = \sqrt{\epsilon + \sigma | \dot{W}(x_1, t) |^2}u^3$ where $Q$ varies randomly according to the Anderson model and the dot represents an derivative operator. Utilizing the method of nonlinear waveguides, it is demonstrated that this equation features linear dispersion properties. This property is leveraged to prove that there is only one possible scattering outcome for solutions with low average energy. Additionally, the method is used to prove that while the outcome is not deterministic, the average energy, not the potential, dictates the possible outcomes. Specifically, the relationship between the potential and the scattering outcomes is found to be non-existent; regardless of Q's randomness and variation, the outcome is the same as for a reference equation. This finding is the first to successfully apply the method of nonlinear waveguides to complex equations involving noise and nonlinear interactions.

To assess the impact of migration on COVID-19 spread, we developed two models. The first model considers migration as an additional transmission channel in the destination country. We calculated the net migration rate that wouldn't lead to COVID-19 spread in that country. The second model takes into account that initial cases in the destination country may arise from infections in the origin country. We derived a criterion for selecting the source country that wouldn't result in COVID-19 spread in both the source and destination countries.

We introduce a novel functor, called the authentic Whittaker functor, which arises from a specific combination of a preimage under the quantum affine reflection and a module restriction.  It has been demonstrated that this functor yields a two-sided equivalence of categories when applied sequentially to the module categories of the centralizer and the quantum group.  Furthermore, the resulting categories are comprised of Harish-Chandra modules for the maximal torus.  Utilizing the framework of the algebraic nature of the Whittaker model, we are able to obtain a novel proof of the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality.  This involves showing that the invariants of the group action on the space of twisted quantum affine Lie algebras have a simple description as the constitutive parts of the authentic Whittaker functor.

The SiD experiment sensor package is designed to capture precise interactions between high-energy particles, with a significant focus on the si sensor. A proposed modification to the SiD sensor concept aims to enhance the detector's capability in specific, high-energy particle collision scenarios, with key aspects of this modification being outlined.

To investigate if tetrahedron-based structures in amorphous ices can form hexagonal ice (Ih) and low-density amorphous ice (LDA), we've simulated high-pressure conditions on atomic and molecular ices in an NVT nanosecond molecular dynamics simulation. Specifically, our studies on high-pressure deuterated LDA (LDA-D) found no transition to the hexagonal structure (Ih) upon applying 1 GPa of pressure. We've discovered that certain tetrahedron-based connections in both LDA and LDA-D act as "fractures" that weaken under pressure, whereas the ice rings in both materials are equally resilient against pressure. Conversely, our simulations on high-pressure liquid water (LQ) found a shift towards a more ordered, tetrahedral structure. We believe that certain defects in both LDA and LDA-D hinder their transformation into Ih and LDA-D, respectively. We suggest an adapted theory of crystallization, implying that under external influences, existing connections in both LDA and LDA-D become unstable and lead to a return to the liquid state rather than crystal formation. We believe that since under pressure liquid water forms ordered, tetrahedral connections, it eventually transforms into ice VI and, with an increase in pressure, into the higher-density ice VI-A.

A set of experiments utilized to acquire atomic-level images of various materials and gauge their local electron densities using a STMs equipped with a tungsten tip. These studies considered three target materials: graphite, gold, and silicon. Graphite's structure was clearly visualized based on its characteristic atomic lattice pattern. The experiments then proceeded to evaluate the LDOS of graphite by adjusting the tunneling current while maintaining a set bias voltage. Similar procedures were employed to study the LDOS of gold and silicon. These experiments were carried out in three distinct modes: constant current, constant height, and low bias. Each mode was further explored through a series of experiments at varying sample and tip voltages. These studies aimed to understand the influence of electron charge accumulation on the sample surfaces. These experiments provided new insights, especially in terms of understanding the impact of gold's work function on its electronic properties. These studies also shed light on the influence of electron charge accumulation on the sample surfaces. These experiments clearly demonstrated the effectiveness of STMs in mapping atomic-level structures and assessing electronic densities within materials.

The integration of automated formal methods and machine learning is highly
anticipated self-improvement. The diverse nature of established methods for
formal proof requires careful selection and application. This paper presents a
novel approach to enhancing the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs by introducing
a compact theorems library and a proof bank. The proposed system leverages
theorem matching and proof search, offering a compact solution. A thorough
evaluation of the approach demonstrates its effectiveness and practicality in
both reducing and verifying proof obligations. Additionally, this work explores
potential strategies for incorporating machine learning, streamlining proof search,
and reconstructing proofs.

Space missions rely heavily on radio communication with Earth, and radio waves are used to study planetary magnetospheres. Researchers analyze the magnetospheric environment by converting time series data into various representations of wave patterns. This process relies on data manipulation rather than raw data analysis. Our goal is to develop an approach that makes the magnetospheric environment more intuitive to interpret, focusing on detecting and visualizing wave patterns through feature engineering techniques. By applying our methods to actual MMS data from the Trailing Edge of the Magnetospheric Cusp event in 2015, we achieved notable results, significantly surpassing existing techniques in wave pattern detection, revealing more precise and complex patterns in the process.

A specific type of dilaton black membrane with rotation and no charge, derived from a higher-dimensional Kaluza-Klein process, is considered. When a supertranslational scalar field is included, the resulting dilaton black membrane has a unique temperature, but one that doesn't follow a specific thermodynamic relation. However, when a specific type of nonlinear electromagnetic field is added, the resulting configuration becomes thermally stable and follows traditional thermodynamic properties. Specifically, this configuration adheres to a fundamental thermodynamic principle known as the first law, and its study shows that the addition of this nonlinear electromagnetic field corrects the temperature's relation to entropy. Moreover, when the black membrane's area is used to define entropy instead of the dilaton, the resulting system exhibits a thermodynamically complete set of parameters, and its study shows that the addition of this nonlinear electromagnetic field leads to a greater thermodynamic stability.

The symbolic execution framework is a computer science technique used for driving the development of intelligent systems, with the focus being on developing methods that closely resemble the natural way of human thinking. One of the fundamental problems that symbolic execution aims to solve is the challenge of text understanding, with the representation of language as a network of concepts at its core. This network connects words and phrases based on their semantic relationships, with the computation of these connections being declarative in nature. Unlike traditional methods that rely on neural networks and are inherently implicit, the current state-of-the-art framework relies on logical structures that can be modified using logical operators. However, the process of updating these text representations on the fly, much like human memory recall, poses a significant challenge to declarative methods. This task involves retrieving concepts from memory and making instant connections between words and their meanings. This task requires a system with rapid information retrieval capabilities, even with the level of detail being dynamically adjusted. This task of balancing detail and context has been achieved in human-like recall through the development of a framework that utilises on-the-fly information retrieval from conceptual databases using declarative operations. The framework uses memory consolidation mechanisms, with the level of detail presented being dynamically adjusted based on the context and interconnections between concepts being adjusted in real-time. The effectiveness of this innovative approach was demonstrated in the context of textual processing, with the level of detail in detailed stories and news articles being automatically adjusted to meet the needs of the reader.

Both CCR and CAR algebras can be represented within a unified framework through the incorporation of a specific linear map into a Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra, thereby establishing analogues for Bohr type algebras as previously defined by Luty in [J. Austral. Math. 61 (1997) 335-346].

This work presents an explicit semantics for GP 2 programs with a reduced number of execution steps. Initially, existing GP 2 semantics by Kahn and Sittig is recapped before providing an alternative, more straightforward transformation that yields a minor-step semantics. Further analysis compares the new semantics with existing ones and highlights its distinct nature along with potential advantages and disadvantages.

Theories suggest that young stars may have their disk materials depleted by intense X-ray and ultraviolet radiation, causing gas to be lost through mass outflows or dispersed into interstellar space. Additionally, young stars may also have their magnetic fields transmit energy and mass from their disks to surrounding space, releasing it in the form of plasmas and particles. Studies predict this disk activity should result in detectable radio emissions. The aim of this study is to assess the likelihood of these predictions being true by analyzing the case of TW Hydrae, a young star with extensive X-ray and ultraviolet radiation emissions. Theoretical models of disk loss through outflows and radiation suggest that TW Hydrae's disk should be depleted of certain gas isotopes if these processes are occurring. The study found these gas isotopes to be depleted, but not to the extent predicted by disk loss models, which places these models at odds with observational data. The study further analyzes potential radio emissions resulting from disk loss models and compares them to those resulting from magnetic field interactions with the disk. The study finds that TW Hydrae does not emit any significant radio emissions, which contrasts with the predictions of intense emissions from disk loss models, but aligns with the predictions of magnetic field interactions with the disk. The study suggests that TW Hydrae's disk is likely being shaped by the effects of magnetic field interactions with the disk rather than intense X-ray and ultraviolet radiation emissions. We have found all factorizations of the Chebyshev polynomial variants $U_d(x)-a^2$ for $d$ up to 100 and some specific polynomials $U_{11}(x)-U_{11}(1)$, as well as all factorizations of the Chetti-Dahan-Vidal variants $U_d(x)-a^2 U_{2k}(x)$ for $k$ up to 100. Notably, these polynomials $U_d(x)$ satisfy minimal equations $\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{d}\right)$. We also present some additional factorizations. These were obtained using the "Minimal Equations" technique initially developed in a study by the same authors. The found factorizations can be used in various applications, such as in the evaluation of definite integrals and the investigation of trisection properties of Chebyshev polynomials.

The widespread adoption of Smart Grid technology, along with the increasing demand for power, has led to the need for advanced transformer capabilities. The proposed Transient Stable Region Analyzer (TSTAR) allows designers to optimize the design parameters of a Symmetric Phase Angle Modulating (SPAM) transformer to ensure stability during oscillatory states. The paper presents a new design approach that utilizes SPAM with reduced complexity, thereby reducing the risk of instability and safely shuts down the system when it reaches its limits. The paper also introduces an approach to categorize and identify transient behaviors in SPAM reactors. The proposed SPAM design not only meets power system stability standards but also complies with standard electrical regulations. The research also proposes a method to identify and understand transient behaviors in SPAM reactors. The effectiveness and performance of the proposed SPAM design is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical case studies. The research provides a foundation for SPAM reactors to be used in real-world power systems and electrical devices. The analysis provides valuable insights for SPAM reactor design and function.

The high bandwidths offered by mmWave spectrum are well-suited for supporting high-data-rate services such as virtual reality and augmented reality. To effectively utilize this spectrum, network operators must implement orthogonal resource allocation to minimize interference between concurrent transmissions.  With the aid of artificial intelligence, or machine learning, more profitable resource allocations can be achieved.  However, existing machine learning-based methods that apply this principle to mmWave networks, which divide the spectrum into frequency bands and divide up these into smaller parts called subchannels, do not always achieve success.  Users in these networks can only receive data that is sent to specific groups of users and an algorithm, or the model that creates these groups, does not always achieve optimal results.  To address the issue, a new method, called the Hybrid Encoding Approach, was developed.  To train this new method, data from mmWave networks was gathered and two parts were created.  The first part was designed to create different groups of users and the second part was created to optimize the different parts or subchannels in these groups.  The model was trained using data from these parts and when put to the test, achieved better results than similar models, or the models that created the groups and subchannels.

For any finite group $G$ and integer $n$, we define the set $\Gamma(G,n)$ as the smallest subgroup of the automorphism group of a free group of rank $n$ that contains all finitely supported automorphisms. Considering the central extension $\widetilde{\Gamma}(G,n)$ of $\Gamma(G,n)$ by its centre, we focus on the residual finiteness properties of the quasi-isometry class of $\Gamma(G,n)$. Importantly, if $G$ is a virtually residually finite group, we prove that $\Gamma(G,n)$ has a similar property, making $\Gamma(G,n)$ and hence also its product with any group residual over $G$, an $R$-group. Moreover, our findings extend to certain metabelian groups of the same nature.

We explored the long-term behavior of a bar made of different materials connected in a star pattern, and we examined how the system evolves over time by considering the movement of all its parts simultaneously. Using an innovative approach, we developed an in-depth understanding of the system's dynamics, and we showed that it could be accurately represented using a specific mathematical model consisting of interconnected, interconnected ordinary differential equations. Based on this model, we determined the conditions under which the system would return to its initial state, and we found that this condition depends on the connections between the different parts of the system. Finally, we discussed how the system's behavior changes in response to various system parameters.

Recent studies have highlighted several nuclei that require examination in order to accurately investigate r-process nucleosynthesis, a topic of significant interest. In this research, we have combined existing experimental data and energy-respectful theoretical calculations to forecast additional properties of those nuclei. The predictions made in this research have reached levels of accuracy not seen before in nuclear data, and in this research we explain how the machine-learning framework that enabled such accuracy was developed. The predicted data includes the ground-state field, energy of excitation, energy of rotation, quadrupole energy, one-neutron separation energy, and one- and two-proton separation energies. The predicted data was generated using the Reinforcement Neural Network algorithm, trained against a training set that included 616 measured nuclear energy levels, including ~200 highly accurate entries, a quantity typically considered sufficient to prevent the appearance of biases. The research against r-process nuclei has utilized the predicted data to investigate r-process star models, a topic of great interest due to the sudden nature in which r-process elements appear in the star models. The research finds that the nature of r-process nuclei to be the way in which the nuclear shell closes, a topic of great interest due to the overall trend. High-precision superconducting devices used in quantum computing research are vulnerable to minute variations in their operating environment, variations which encompass temperature, mechanical stress, and electromagnetic radiation. To ensure the successful execution of quantum coding procedures at the superconducting qubit level, it is crucial to regulate and stabilize these factors. This work involves an innovative technique for assessing and stabilizing the dielectric loss in high-quality (Al$_2$O$_3$) ceramic used in the capacitors of superconducting qubits, employing an advanced measurement approach that exploits the phenomenon of parametric amplification to detect variations in dielectric loss at an extremely sensitive scale of billions of parts per million. This improved measurement technique demonstrates dielectric loss levels below 0.1 ppm/$^2$ in 0.2 mm thick (Al$_2$O$_3$) samples at room temperature, representing an enhancement of over two orders of magnitude when compared to the best existing measurements at lower temperatures. To accomplish this improved measurement, the authors employed an inbuilt amplifier with a highly sensitive response to input signals, specifically designed to the standards of the quantum domain, which non-trivially enhances the accuracy of measurements across multiple parameters including thermal, mechanical, and electromagnetic stabilities.

The phenomenon of electro-optical modulation allows us to study the interplay between an optical field and a material's electronic structure. This interplay is influenced by specific molecular bonds that give rise to observable optical effects. A particular concern in this context is the pull-apart effect, where certain modulator fingers exhibit an anomalous decrease in resonance frequency, but upon closer examination, this phenomenon is found to be the result of an incorrect calculation derived from a simplistic model. Through advanced mathematical representations of molecular bonds, it's revealed that the anomalous behavior is merely a consequence of a standard phenomenon.

This study develops a novel reformulation and solution strategy for a robust optimization problem with two stages that takes into account uncertain constraints and binary dependencies. In particular, the two-stage model is designed to minimize the most severe cost impacts resulting from combinations of binary and non-binary decision variables on system limits. By converting the original bilinear optimization problem into an equivalent Lagrangian dual form, our method yields a tractable convex optimization problem with certain special properties. In contrast to traditional approaches, our formulation introduces new dual variables that can exploit variable dependencies, including those related to binary decisions. In addition to offering significant computational advantages, our method allows for the easy incorporation of various optimization models, including linear, quadratic, and convex models. In order to further improve solution efficiency, our method takes advantage of problem symmetry by leveraging Benders' cutting plane approach. In particular, in scenarios where one stage of the optimization problem involves binary decisions, our method can significantly reduce computational complexity by applying select cutting planes and proving theoretical bounds on duality gaps. In order to validate the efficacy of our solution strategy, we conducted extensive numerical experiments on a variety of test problems, including scenarios with contingent corridor problems, supply chain optimization problems, and multi-stage investment problems involving binary and non-binary decisions. In particular, our results demonstrate that our solution strategy can achieve a high level of accuracy, with duality gaps never exceeding 0.56% and an average duality gaps of 0.16%. The diversity of datasets plays a significant role in the advancement of machine learning techniques. This paper introduces the H4M dataset, which encompasses various dimensions in Beijing, allowing for a more comprehensive research approach. The H4M dataset consists of five distinct categories, which are characterized by different data attributes: a comprehensive demographic profile, a vast network of transportation systems, a combination of air and noise pollution data, a detailed spatial outline of the city's streets and neighborhoods, and a vast collection of images taken from Google Street View. The H4M dataset is uniquely structured to facilitate the execution of numerous research studies, including experiments involving transfer learning, multi-faceted machine learning, and the analysis of diverse demographic profiles. The dataset is accessible through a link provided in the paper's supplementary materials.

One major challenge facing data analysis tools is handling massive datasets effectively, particularly when designing visual templates to uncover hidden patterns and correlations within complex data. Existing tools have limitations, as they often struggle to scale when processing large datasets, leading to difficulties in identifying relevant patterns. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative solution that leverages a visual template-driven method for analyzing complex data. By accommodating various template types and design complexities, our approach optimizes data exploration and pattern detection, especially when dealing with datasets that are not naturally grouped by their characteristics. Additionally, we demonstrate the superiority of our method through comparative studies and showcase its applications in real-world scenarios.

The success of graph neural networks in numerous applications has opened up new possibilities for these models to be used in real-world scenarios, especially in data that is non-Euclidean in nature and non-linear. One significant benefit of neural networks is their ability to utilize knowledge gained from addressing similar problems in other domains, a phenomenon referred to as transfer learning. The vast array of available graph datasets presents a diverse range of problems for models to solve, thereby increasing the likelihood that some datasets contain similar patterns and structures to other, often in other domains. Despite being a crucial aspect of machine learning, there is a lack of research on transfer learning for graph neural networks. In our study, we utilize statistical and comparative analysis to gain insight into transfer learning in graph neural networks, with a particular focus on graph neural networks, specifically GNNs. We evaluate the applicability of numerous widely-used graph neural network models, with over 80 different configurations, on 7 diverse datasets. Our research reveals that experience gained from processing node attributes, especially when they consist of a combination of text information and numerical values, is highly valuable in GNN models that employ relational inductive reasoning. In contrast, the transfer of knowledge from models that are trained on related tasks or with similar characteristics is not as substantial.

Recommending diverse and relevant content to users is the primary function of a suggestion system. The system's task is to identify and suggest items that align with the user's interests and preferences in order to keep them actively engaged. Our proposal is a novel suggestion system centered on a Dual Feature Distribution model, which models the probability of specific items being of interest to a user by taking into account two key characteristics - user-generated content (comments) and system ratings. The probability of interest is assessed for each user-item combination in an explicit manner. The strength of an user-item connection is compared to that of a randomly selected user-item pair, as measured by a tailored comparison metric. The top-rated suggestions are then presented to the user. Our model has been successfully tested using data from a real-world movie rating system, with results demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately identifying relevant suggestions, particularly in scenarios where less user information is available. The model's accuracy was evaluated through both qualitative and quantitative methods.

The problem of disjoint set membership, previously known as "unshuffling sets," involves determining the elements of a set $S$ given that each pair of sets $I$ and $S-I$ are provided, where $I \subseteq S$. A novel proof approach is presented for the known theorem stating that a $O(\log N)$-size decision tree can solve the disjoint set membership problem for any set of $N$ indices. It is further demonstrated that this result leads to a straightforward $O(\log N)$-size data stream algorithm for solving the disjoint set membership problem. This algorithm uses essentially the same approach as many prior solutions but provides a simpler implementation.

The spin susceptibility of Heisenberg magnets in the paramagnetic stage was found to have a non-analytic momentum dependence. This was used to calculate the critical exponents within the momentum expansion framework. It was determined that the non-analytic momentum dependence affects the critical exponents related to $\rho(0)$ and $\alpha$ but not $\Delta$ and $\nu$. The self-consistent mass correction approach also yielded similar exponents without considering the non-analytic momentum dependence. This indicated that the critical behavior of Heisenberg magnets could be accurately described by the momentum-dependent effective model.

The discovery of three-body interaction in multi-particle systems has a significant influence on various scientific disciplines. In waveguide cavity systems, it enables the management of optical modes through atomic multi-diffraction processes. This concept of multi-diffraction introduces novel methods for capturing, manipulating, and trapping atoms. It also facilitates the realization of atomic lattice structures with unique characteristics and allows for the storage of photons within atomic media. This research discusses the multi-diffraction processes in waveguide cavities and presents a design for a device that achieves single-atom capture, manipulation, and measurement. It also outlines a method to implement multi-atom arrays with engineered interactions, serving as a foundational technique for quantum nanophotonics and optical processing systems.

The magnetization of a two-dimensional electron system in a magnetic field is studied,
with specific focus on the Hall conductivity. When considering the linear response,
the strong-field magnetic moment is equivalent to the two-dimensional electron system's
Hall conductivity. However, in the context of this study, the strong-field magnetic moment
refers to the minimum magnetic field required for the electronic ground state to shift,
causing a finite Hall conductivity. It was discovered that in systems close to equilibrium,
this occurs at a finite magnetic field, with the difference between the Hall conductivity
in these states and their counterparts at zero magnetic field directly proportional
to the displacement potential. Furthermore, this study explores the relationship
between the nonlinear Hall conductivity and the ground state's wave function asymmetry,
showing it to be consistent in various nonlinear responses. Lastly, this study examines
how correlation forces affect the system and finds that in the context of this study,
these forces suppress the ground state's asymmetry. It was also theoretically derived
that in systems exhibiting chaos the magnetic moment displays characteristics of a multifractal,
with the study going on to compute the fractal dimensions of the magnetic moment.
It was also discovered that in systems where electron-electron interactions can be ignored,
the magnetic moment's fractal dimensions equal 1.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to the deployment of double-bed hospitals, which typically lack in audio quality, making it challenging for healthcare staff to communicate effectively during life-or-death situations. To enhance dual-patient conferencing, we conducted a study on the effects of immediate speech understanding in critical care settings, including post-intubation care for COVID-19 patients. By leveraging neural networks and a significant dataset of over 200 hours of recordings, we found that superior models significantly outperformed lower-ranking ones by 26.27% and 36.51% in terms of error rates. The best-performing model consisted of 9 layers with a 256-unit hidden population. Notably, we discovered that improving the error rate did not always translate to improvements in convergence speed. The high error rates of existing models, including our top model, did not significantly impede clinical operations for healthcare professionals, as they adapted to the audio quality despite the inaccuracies.

We define a bicritical map as a rational function of degree $d \geq 7$ whose indifferent points separate the Riemann sphere into four components, with each component having positive genus. Our objective is to determine the group of symmetries for the images created by repeatedly applying such maps to specific points on the Riemann sphere. Notably, we found numerous examples of bicritical maps with various degrees and a specified domain on the Riemann sphere, whose group of symmetries is the dihedral group, also known as the dicyclic group D_{2n-1}$, or the 2-group 2\Omega_{2n-1}$. Moreover, we found instances where the degree of the bicritical map divides $2$ but not $3$, resulting in the images having a group of symmetries as trivial. We also showed that the previously identified bicritical maps with such properties are the only ones exhibiting these characteristics. To achieve this, we employed techniques from the theory of branching covers, also incorporating some computational methods. We derived a challenge in this context, specifically addressing whether there are any bicritical maps whose images have a group of symmetries as non-abelian.

Two-dimensional semiconducting materials, specifically transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), have garnered significant attention in both theoretical and experimental studies due to their unique characteristics. The layer-dependent behavior of TMDs allows their electronic properties to be studied across multiple layers, which is particularly important for designing and optimizing devices. This study focuses on the layer-dependent electrostatic potential, a crucial factor in semiconductor devices, in 2D TMDs made of molybdenum (Mo) and tungsten (W), as well as their p-type variants. To accurately assess the potential, we utilized the ab initio quantum mechanics methods, including both DFT and GW calculations. The findings show that the layer-dependent behavior of the potential in these 2D materials is influenced by the single particle excitations. To further analyze this, we calculated the work function, a single-layer property, as well as ionization energy and electron affinity, which are closely related to the electrostatic potential. The results obtained from GW calculations indicate that the electron affinity values are consistent from a one-layer perspective, which is in line with the experimental findings. However, the computational data from DFT and GW show that the electron affinity values converge at certain thickness levels. Additionally, we investigated the electron attraction, which is influenced by the charge distribution within the layers, as well as the forces holding the charge within the layers.
