Previous studies indicate that midbrain activity in humans is primarily associated with the dopaminergic reward prediction error signal in active learning situations. However, our research also demonstrates that midbrain activity in humans is not only responsive to wins and losses during active learning, as predicted by the reinforcement learning model, but also reflects on and adjusts its response to prediction errors in both active and passive learning environments. Notably, both suboptimal and optimal models for adjusting behavior in response to these errors exhibit similar patterns of activity. Furthermore, our data suggest that a wide range of reinforcement learning algorithms, which vary in their approach to updating their internal models for action outcomes, can all potentially influence midbrain activity in humans. This finding implies that midbrain activity may reflect a more general signal related to the learning process itself, rather than being uniquely indicative of an optimal model for updating the likelihood of future outcomes following specific actions.

Recent research on the Hilbert space model of physical systems, primarily based on real algebras, has led to discoveries regarding quantum entanglement and contextuality. However, these findings may not adequately represent the complexifications of these systems, which have deeper mathematical connections. This article explores the potential implications of these connections if quantum systems are truly fundamental to reality, suggesting that the complexifications could provide a more comprehensive framework for understanding quantum phenomena.

The Fréchet distance between two curves can be considered as a measure of how similar they are in terms of their overall shape. For curves represented as sequences of points, the Fréchet distance can be computed based on the paths of corresponding points. A data structure known as the Fréchet filter allows for efficient identification of closest curves in a set. Researchers have proposed filters with logarithmic query times, but these come with a higher time complexity for processing queries. In this study, we investigate the trade-offs between time and query complexity. First, we develop a data structure with sub-quadratic construction cost that offers sub-logarithmic query times and logarithmic disk time complexity. Second, we present an approximate Nearest Neighbor search algorithm under the Fréchet distance, which uses a ball tree-like data structure, allowing for faster query times at the cost of potential errors. The potential errors can be minimized through the use of additional preprocessing steps, which do not affect our time complexity results.

High-precision particle colliders face a major obstacle in their experiments: random errors affecting the measurement of key particles, which hampers their ability to discover new physics. A solution, or at least a workaround, can be found in the form of a method to correct for these errors. This method draws on the principles of medical imaging techniques and has been successfully applied to two real-world collider experiments.

The integration of multiple robotic platforms, each equipped with unique capabilities, presents an opportunity for enhanced collaborative performance in complex and time-sensitive tasks. By developing a unified system to coordinate the actions of these systems, the limitations of individual autonomy can be supplemented with the benefits of collective autonomy. This paper proposes a decentralized, game-theory inspired approach for collective autonomy in mixed-technology environments. It outlines a general framework for task division and coordination, as well as detailed procedures for managing communication and conflict resolution. Key aspects of this framework demonstrate the feasibility of collective autonomy among diverse systems, with experiments demonstrating successful task coordination among platforms with varying capabilities and limitations, even in the presence of communication constraints and system disparities.

For people with visual impairments, accessing digital maps can be a significant challenge. In unfamiliar areas, even sighted individuals face difficulties with standard maps. To address these issues, we suggest an innovative solution: creating a customizable and dynamic map system that accommodates the needs of blind users. Our proposed navigation system is built around a unique diagram called HiTMap, which is composed of interrelated geometric shapes (polygons) that provide an overview of the environment and detailed information about specific regions. To develop HiTMap, we developed an algorithm that generates the diagram by identifying and grouping spatial features in a way that minimizes user confusion. Our system also includes specialized audio displays and navigation tools, including a sound-based interface that utilizes 3D audio cues and an audible turn-by-turn guidance system. To test the effectiveness of HiTMap, we conducted a study involving actual-world experiments in unfamiliar environments, comparing the user experience with HiTMap and Google Street View. The results of this study, with 16 participant blind volunteers, showed that HiTMap enabled faster and more efficient navigation, as well as significantly reduced confusion. Moreover, participant feedback indicated a strong preference for our system over the Google Street View alternative.

Inter-group code sets, comprising group codes with distinct letter combinations, were studied to accommodate various word lengths and numbering systems. Building upon this foundation, a novel extension to inter-group code sets was proposed, involving the incorporation of additional, specialized code sets to address exceptional cases, thus ensuring all possible combinations are accounted for. Inter-group supplementary code sets can be realized with Z-arrays, where each variable is governed by a distinct mapping. The paper also introduces a comprehensive set of two-dimensional Z-supplementary array code sets, where each variable, governed by distinct mappings, collectively forms a unique combination. These novel code sets are expected to play a crucial role in addressing unique constraints.

We introduce a nonconvex variational framework for CT image reconstruction that incorporates multiple energy levels, accounts for noise and signal breakdown, which is particularly effective against the effects of rare earth metals in medical scans. Our model utilizes weighted least squares with weights determined by quasi-Newton methods to counter signal degradation, resulting in robust outcomes even with weight initializations. Our experiments show superior image quality and reliable weight values compared to conventional methods.

To investigate the role of electron counterflow and nonlocality on the dynamical structure of the electron liquid in the case of low separations, we used a hydrodynamic model incorporating these factors alongside Coulomb and kinetic energy contributions. Assuming a hydrodynamic description that takes a wave length of around 10 nanometers or lower as a starting point, our analysis demonstrated the interplay between the electron liquid's energy gaps under electron counterflow and nonlocality. It was found that electron counterflow induces a significant negative frequency shift of the gap modes while increasing their intensity. Moreover, our model revealed the appearance of additional energy gaps at certain wave numbers. The implementation of a nonlocal model, however, resulted in the closure of the energy gaps at extremely small separations, accompanied by a shift towards the low frequency range. An analytical approximation of the energy dispersion in the local model revealed the association of the lower frequency shift with the formation of gap-plasmons composed of electrons from the surface and conduction band, referred to as S-gap-plasmons and C-gap-plasmons. The corresponding dispersion relationships, specifically -0.3-0.4 eV for S-gap-plasmons and -0.5-0.6 eV for C-gap-plasmons, were determined. The proposed model offers a practical route for measuring the electron liquid's fundamental characteristics, specifically its energy gaps, at the nanoscale.

Research has shown that contextual word representations hold valuable information for identifying the characteristics of named entities. This paper explores how important the context is for named entity recognition and develops an approach, Contextual NER, that utilizes attention to the surrounding context for both entity type and boundary predictions. To enhance context understanding, we also introduce an adaptive importance weighting mechanism that forces the model to prioritize relevant words. This novel approach underpins the CPER model, a contextual predictor that makes predictions informed by the critical information within each sentence. Evaluations conducted on the BERT-ANER dataset confirm CPER's superiority over current leading models.

This study addresses the challenge of designing an interactive interface for visualizing complex, multi-dimensional time series data that coexists with linear data. To foster engagement on screens, we explored the use of comparative studies, analyzed user behavior, and incorporated thoughtfully crafted interactions. As a contribution, we present Compass Link, a dashboard display that seamlessly integrates time series and linear data, enhancing user experience. Key design elements of Compass Link include its unique triangular layout, distinctive visual indicators, and innovative transitions between different types of data. Comprehensive user studies confirmed that Compass Link effectively facilitates engagement and showcases its practical applications in data exploration.

The advent of electronic health records has driven the development of health informatics, enabling the analysis of health-related data to aid diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. As health-related data has increased in diversity, both in structure and type, and has become increasingly scattered across various sources, the need for more advanced analysis methods has arisen. Our study proposes a novel method for utilizing graph neural networks to analyze digital health records by incorporating multiple aspect vectors. In testing this method's ability to analyze diverse health-related data, we employed a node classification task and compared our results to those obtained from a standard attention-based graph neural network and a BERT-based pre-training approach. Our findings indicate that by leveraging the inherent organizational structure of digital health records, the diversity of the data itself can be minimized, and the performance of our method can surpass that of traditional neural network-based systems. Specifically, our method achieved more accurate node classification results on two real-world MIMIC-II datasets.

Within the framework of the soft interface model, the profile of solvents interacting with a charge-modulated interface is investigated using a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, taking into account the impact of solvent polarization. It is demonstrated that solvent polarization has a substantial effect on the charge distribution within the interface and neighboring regions. Moreover, under certain conditions, multiple discrete charge peaks emerge close to the interface, separated by regions of nearly zero charge. The relationship between the resulting charge distribution and the applied voltage is then studied as the system transitions into the overload regime. The results of this study reveal that solvent polarization is a primary factor responsible for the observed quantized charge peaks. The absence of certain transitions, such as the Bikerman or Schrifrier phases, is attributed to the inherent properties of the system, characterized by the presence of multiple layers of ions near the interface. The possibility of observing the overdraft phase in experiments on soft interfaces is also explored.

Understanding the capabilities of machines through software development is contingent upon explicit, unambiguous specification. This process is particularly challenging when attempting to comprehend complex, dynamic systems. In this research, we explore how natural language processing can enhance specification by analyzing text-based descriptions of software systems, focusing on dynamic memory allocation as a primary objective. Rather than expecting formal, domain-specific terminology in development workflows, we advocate for a more flexible approach that leverages language processing to extract and clarify specification details from a wide range of sources, including those with varying levels of organization and technical proficiency.

This research proposes a novel energy-efficient relaying technique called joint relay scheduling and power control through network coding (JRSPC-NC). A single scheduling cycle is specifically designed to include all users and multiple relays with low energy consumption to maintain connectivity in case of direct link failure. To achieve this, we use a two-stage approach that includes a scheduling phase with high power and a broadcasting phase using low power and network coding by the relays to reduce overall network energy consumption. To prove its efficiency, we establish a lower bound on the energy savings achieved by JRSPC-NC and demonstrate its practical applicability by comparing it to traditional approaches in real-world scenarios.

The electron spin behavior on niobium surfaces influenced by magnetic impurities has been studied using theoretical insights from Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) theories involving impurities and dimer impurities. By considering YSR states as distinct initial conditions for many-body systems in a time-dependent framework, it became clear that YSR states experience spin relaxation within ultra-short timescales. Furthermore, the presence of multiple YSR states on niobium surfaces further accelerates relaxation, and their resonance influences spin relaxation within dimer impurities composed of magnetic elements. The theoretical findings on niobium surfaces supporting magnetic impurities align with the hypothesis that quantum coherent YSR states contribute to impurity-based magnetic second harmonic generation.

A novel search for the rare Kaon decay in motion is reported on, specifically for the process $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$. The analysis utilized data gathered by the NA62 experiment at CERN's Proton Proton Collider in 2009 with an incident $10^19$ proton beam, and an energy threshold of $75\GeV$. This study aimed to detect the decay in motion of $K^+$ kaons as they travel through a 750 mm thick regime of 4$\%$ magnetic field, and to estimate their maximum lab momentum. A comparison with the expected background was made between two groups of particles, and by combining statistical and systematic uncertainties, a upper bound of $10^{-10}$ was set for the branching ratio at 90$\%$ confidence level.

Current distribution-to-distribution scan alignment approaches struggle with
prejudice in their assumptions about data distribution, model, and label, leading
to poor performance and inaccurate estimates. To address this issue, we
propose a novel method which involves training a Deep Neural Network filter
capable of detecting and correcting bias in data without making any prior
assessments about the data. Our solution is two-fold: first, we derive an
expression to gauge the level of prejudice in any distribution; second, we
develop a robust algorithm to train the DNN filter, which can effectively
rectify prejudice in any system. Our method is universally applicable and
does not rely on specific data or environment settings.

Satellite images hold considerable value in various fields such as cartography, urban planning, and geology. However, the processing of these images poses significant challenges due to their large size and the diversity of features present in them. The design of systems capable of efficiently analyzing such data is crucial for numerous applications, particularly in real-time environments where the use of deep learning methods may not be practical. The present work aims to address this issue by describing a basic image processing pipeline that utilizes a straightforward edge detection algorithm. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its application to datasets at the Kaggle Competitions 'Planet: Analyze this! (2016)' and 'GNN for Planet! (2018)'. The results obtained indicate that simple techniques can produce satisfactory outcomes in feature extraction, while the diversity within satellite datasets makes the application of specialized methods for specific tasks desirable. The diversity within satellite datasets makes the application of specialized methods for specific tasks desirable.

A comprehensive framework is developed to characterize the signal development over time for a specific absorption edge in an analysis process that relies on micro-bunching patterns of low-energy electrons. The pattern's initial distribution is assumed to be even, and as it travels through a strong magnetic field, it undergoes non-linear changes resulting in the energy extraction of photons at a particular absorption edge. The research presents a series of fundamental equations that govern the growth of electron clusters over time, and an approximation is made for a specific type of absorption process. The accuracy of the proposed model is evaluated through comparisons with detailed simulations and experimental data on a particular copper sample surface. The framework is found to be effective in understanding the initial stages of signal development and can be utilized to improve the detection of specific absorption edges.

Neural networks are highly susceptible to even the slightest corruption, making them vulnerable to manipulation. This vulnerability can be leveraged by malicious agents to exploit and deceive AI models, leading to potential misuse. To prevent such attacks, generating random noise within the neural network can be an effective defense mechanism, akin to masking the signal. This method can be utilized in the input layer or integrated into the network through the creation of hybrid generative adversarial networks. To further increase model resilience, blending random noise into existing data is another effective technique. This research develops and introduces the concept of blend GANs as a means of producing high-quality mixed images for enhancing the robustness of the modulation categorization model against malicious assaults. This approach is tested and compared using the BAI, CMSS, DAI, and CIA benchmarks.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a crucial process that needs to be done precisely and efficiently to contribute to research and clinical decision-making. Most current models for segmentation have been trained on a single, publicly available dataset that is labeled "intra-reliably." This study assesses the effectiveness of continuous learning on an unsupervised dataset and a previously trained model on a new test dataset by evaluating their performance in a standard segmentation task. Surprisingly, the results show that training models on smaller datasets with more aggressive data augmentation results in similar or even better performance compared to training on the larger, more familiar dataset. This finding opens up new possibilities for research directions that prioritize using multiple sources of data to enhance the accuracy of clinical decision-making.

Contrast is a visual effect that attracts human attention across a wide spectrum of colors. Research has most extensively examined the attention-grabbing properties of contrast within the black-white color space. However, multi-dimensional color spaces have also drawn interest due to their ability to encompass a broader range of colors and their applications in color categorization and naming. This study focuses on the attention-grabbing properties of contrast within the 3D manic color space, which is defined as the set of colors defined by $\frac{r}{g}$ ratios greater than 1, where r and g are red and green color channel values, respectively. The study finds that contrast in the manic color space, defined as the difference in color properties, can effectively predict the diversity of natural images' color palettes. Moreover, it surpasses black-white contrast in its ability to do so.

The development of accurate predictive models in complex systems is a crucial yet challenging task that necessitates quantifying uncertainty in probabilistic forecasts. This issue is particularly prominent in areas such as climate science, meteorology, and epidemiology. This study employs error growth dynamics to investigate how predictions and uncertainty in dynamical systems evolve over time. By analyzing how fundamental nonlinear structures like feedback loops and switches influence predictive uncertainty, we demonstrate the various forms error growth dynamics can take. This investigation also utilizes applications in disease modeling and weather forecasting to illustrate the utility of this framework for assessing model uncertainty and developing intelligent machine learning systems that minimize it.

The formation of massive stars requires a critical minimum amount of time to develop within massive, self-gravitating molecular gas cores. Recent observations of dark nebulae using Dragon, a high-resolution camera at the Calar Alto observatory, have allowed us to precisely measure the core separation in molecular clouds. These data show that cores in massive star-forming regions expand at the same rate as in regions forming lower-mass stars, indicating that massive star formation is not accelerated by core pressure. Since cores in these regions tend to have lower densities, the rate of massive star formation is likely limited by the time it takes for gas and dust to compact, rather than being hindered by the time it takes for stars to form.

Gravitational events from primordial black holes can be studied by observing a star being pulled into its central black hole under specific conditions. The theory of shadow formation is crucial in understanding general relativity, and recent simulations have applied the PopSyCLE code to simulate PBH gravitational waves and a dark matter system. The result is a model where PBHs emit gravitational waves that affect the surrounding dark matter, causing it to oscillate due to a two-body problem, and subsequent collisions between the dark matter particles cause a PBH overdensity that eventually collapses into a black hole. This process can be visualized through 3D animations and a phase diagram that shows stable states in systems with low PBH masses, and indicates collapse in systems with high PBH masses, especially in cases of strong dark matter interactions.

We investigate a system of rigid, wedge-shaped spheres within a two-dimensional plane, where each sphere belongs to an imaginary circle with a specific radius, and the edge of this sphere touches the plane. Variations in the imaginary circle's angle are categorized as growth, splay, and decline. A stage in this system's development is marked by an equal distribution of sphere edge lengths within a set interval. A novel algorithm is employed to calculate the number of development stages and their respective durations as the sphere variations progress. For a given number of spheres, the maximum number of stages possible depends on the number of spheres present in the sphere model, whereas if the number of spheres is allowed to increase, the number of stages can reach an infinite potential. Furthermore, we graph and analyze the algorithm's output in terms of its dependence on the number of spheres for infinite and finite numbers of stages.

Recent breakthroughs in transfer learning have significantly improved the
performance of NLP models, yet large datasets and sophisticated data mixing 
techniques remain costly in terms of resources. Our study demonstrates the 
feasibility of achieving high-performing results on smaller scales by adopting 
a more efficient approach to data processing. In this approach, complex 
algorithmic components are optimized for unique token adaptations, enabling 
faster training and more efficient results. Our experiments show that this 
strategy can produce better outcomes on adjustment problems compared to the 
standard resources-based approach, particularly in areas such as text 
autocorrect and text autosummary tasks.

The context for set augmentation tasks, which seek to expand a given set with similar items, is typically lacking in existing preference models, which often rely on dot product or learning to rank methods to assign scores and simulate class labels. Meanwhile, aspect-based sentiment analysis has shown significant progress in leveraging external context to improve sentence interpretation, suggesting a non-contextual approach to preference ordering may be insufficient. A novel contrast of two algorithms, one contextual and one non-contextual, is proposed to tackle the set augmentation problem, where the key distinction lies in incorporating external context to extract visual and semantic properties of visual objects. The dual-agency hypothesis is proposed to address the computational challenge of external context, splitting the computational load between the learner and the external context. The proposed algorithms are evaluated against a range of visual objects and external contexts, including images of objects, object properties, and weather conditions, demonstrating the importance of external context through human evaluation. Experimental results confirm that a non-contextual comparison method falls short of the performance of the proposed dual-agentual approach across multiple metrics.

Amorphous solids like glass, which resists deviations from thermal equilibrium, offer a challenging theoretical framework. Nonetheless, empirical investigations into the dynamics and thermodynamics of glass formation remain underrepresented, especially in polymer liquids which exhibit a prolonged transition period. Moreover, the well-documented correlation between heat capacity and structural variation in these liquids does not indicate a direct relationship between thermodynamic and dynamic properties, as one would anticipate based on principles of linear response theory. Notably, the evolution of the dynamics across various time scales in polymer liquids is similarly difficult to explain using linear principles. To address this issue, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the dynamics across multiple time scales in a polymer-bubble system that mimics the glass-forming liquid dynamics. The study revealed that the response to local pressure changes in the polymer-bubble system is primarily linear for minor changes but becomes non-linear for more substantial alterations, which correlates with observed phenomena in actual glass-forming liquids. The findings suggest that the transition from one time scale to another below the alpha relaxation peak is connected to the significant pressure variation within the system, which occurs when it surpasses a certain threshold equivalent to 600 MPa, a factor roughly equivalent to the density difference between amorphous and liquid states in glass-forming materials.

The vast majority of language processing models are trained on data that contains errors, such as incorrect syntactic structures and anomalous word sequences. This research explores how large language models, in particular the Transformer architecture, cope with rejected parses during syntactic analysis, and we find that they often overestimate the likelihood of rejected parses. Building on this insight, we develop a novel sampling mechanism, inspired by partial credit, that rewards models for accurately processing rejected parses. When integrated with this mechanism, which we refer to as rejection sampling with partial credit, there is substantial evidence that models are able to learn from rejected parses and reduce their overestimation of their likelihood. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that models trained with rejection sampling demonstrate more realistic expectations for out-of-sample data and improved performance on downstream parsing tasks. This research is a significant extension of prior work, which focused exclusively on correct parses, and highlights the importance of incorporating rejected parses into language modeling and associated downstream tasks.

The capacity of a language model to generate creative outputs depends on its ability to focus on open-ended topics, for example, writing short stories or poems. Models can misinterpret limited input as a specific subject and fail to expand beyond a narrow understanding. This study investigates whether focusing on a specific aspect, similar to human concentration, can be achieved in a machine context. A new method, called Look-ahead Focus, is presented, allowing models to filter and select details from system-generated outputs during the prediction process. This approach is denoted as post-focus, differentiating it from the traditional pre-focus method where choices are made before generating content. The proposed post-focus technique is evaluated in two areas: multi-step generation and step-by-step text editing. A new, sophisticated dataset is created to assess look-ahead generation in the domain of humorous axioms. The results of the study indicate that the Look-ahead Focus technique leads to the invention of more humorous and relevant axioms when compared to standard methods; furthermore, incorporating human oversight enhances both the quality and creativity of the generated axioms.

  where $\mathbb{T}$ denotes a torus, $R$ represents a Poisson tensor, and $\mathbb{T}$, $R$ are specified in terms of root systems $\mathcal{R}$ and $\mathcal{R}_H$ with dual graphs $G_{\mathcal{R}}$ and $G_{\mathcal{R}_H}$. 
  The formula introduces a new polynomial $a_i(\lambda)$ for each node $i$ in the dual graphs $G_{\mathcal{R}}$ and $G_{\mathcal{R}_H}$, 
  and it shows the connection between the curvature tensor $H$ and the graph structure of the dual graphs $G_{\mathcal{R}}$ and $G_{\mathcal{R}_H}$ through the appearance of the unitary factor $(2\pi i)$ and the degree of the numerators and denominators for the transfer functions $a_i(\lambda)$

We examine the properties of an $N$-component scalar field model in $d$ dimensions with a specific potential dependent on the components' interactions. When the potential's $\lambda d/N$ parameter varies, with $1 \leq \lambda \leq d+1$, the model has a unique universal behavior described by an interacting conformal field theory, applicable in the thermodynamic limit and for any $N$. We find that at criticality, thermal phase information is equivalent to entanglement information in the CFT framework, with the holographic representation having a dual representation in a geometrically flat spacetime-like environment across its minimum volume spatial section with a specific dimension of $d + 2 - \lambda$.

We investigate the model's phase diagram, self-dimension, and critical exponent of specificity $\omega$ across the defined $\lambda$ range. We discover that at large $N$, how quickly entropy decreases with system size is determined by the specificity $\omega$, which in turn depends on an invariable characteristic of the CFT. We find that $\omega > 0$ across the defined $\lambda$ range and that $\omega$ gradually goes from $d$ to 1. We also demonstrate that the CFT self-dimension, with a specific characteristic $\lambda$, has a minimum dimension of $d + 2 - \lambda$. This study aims to build upon Wang et al's structure for pricing Asian options by leveraging one-dimensional diffusion processes instead of more complex Markov processes. It has been discovered, however, that their method can be directly linked to a result initially developed by Benth, Benth, and Schoenmakers. Furthermore, the approach proposed by Wang et al involves calculating a path-dependent average, which can be expressed as a convex combination of one-dimensional diffusion-based solutions depending on specific parameters that adapt to future time advancements. It is noted that such parametric constructions may offer greater practical utility due to the added flexibility in modeling, which can, in fact, extend beyond diffusions to more comprehensive Markov processes as initially suggested by Wang et al.

Using a decade's worth of data from the Large Area Telescope on the Gamma-ray Observatory, researchers have identified a novel gamma-ray phenomenon - high-energy radiation spreading along large cosmic structures, specifically at a rate of approximately 0.75 degrees per gigaparsec, and primarily comprised of photons with energies between 1 and 100 GeV. This phenomenon was observed emanating from groups of galaxies and significant clusters, and its emission pattern demonstrated a strong correlation with the host structures' optical brightness. Notably, the total gamma-ray flux from these observed cosmic structures is consistent with the expected emission pattern, if they were to contribute to the total flux through their respective volumes. Moreover, the observed radiation does not appear to be a result of secondary electrons produced by cosmic rays interacting with gas, and its energy spectrum does not show any variation with energy. Researchers have considered multiple astrophysical interpretations for this novel component, and its significance in relation to the total flux from the Galactic plane. This phenomenon holds significant implications for our understanding of the intergalactic medium. Researchers have applied these findings to establish a rough estimate for the gamma-ray background, and have predicted the detectability of the diffuse gamma-ray emission from smaller structures such as galaxy groups and individual galaxies.

We explore the theory behind initial features in cosmological perturbation theory, particularly how certain features are naturally produced by the cosmological inflation process. During inflation, gravitational waves leave behind distinctive features in the primordial density perturbations that can be characterized by the characteristics of the initial feature, such as its location and shape. Notably, certain features migrate due to the dynamics of the universe, with features related to gravitational waves undergoing a frequency shift that depends on the universe's expansion. This cosmological frequency shift provides a connection between the inflation era, primordial features, and the observations of cosmic large-scale structure. The effect of the cosmological frequency shift on initial features is most pronounced for models of early universe expansion that occur at high energies, such as models of slow-roll de Sitter vacuum states. The characteristics of primordial features, such as their location and shape, can be determined by observing the spectral properties of cosmological perturbations, such as the properties of the primordial power spectrum. The theory of initial features in cosmological perturbation theory offers a framework to understand the properties of primordial features and determine the initial conditions for cosmological perturbation theory.

It is well established that Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) derive their global classification capabilities from local region-specific representations. Researchers have focused on visual features, but the role of semantics is not clearly understood. This paper demonstrates that a novel semantic filter, integrated with a specific architecture of CNNs, is able to produce classification results on par with state-of-the-art models by leveraging both visual and semantic features. The latent semantic filter is capable of being transferred across multiple tasks without undergoing re-training. Additionally, the proposed framework is adept at producing detailed and accurate visual explanations for classification decisions, thereby resolving disputes and uncertainties. The proposed model is capable of producing explanations that are both visual and semantic in nature. The proposed model is capable of producing explanations that are both visual and semantic in nature.

The long-range Van der Waals (VDW) forces play a significant role in determining physical, chemical, and biological properties. Studies of materials with strong electron-phonon interactions, however, have revealed that the inclusion of retuning effects facilitated by phonons significantly modifies the predictions of the long-range London-dipole (LD) model used in calculating VDW interactions, resulting in significant deviations. This research assesses the impact of electronic-phononic red-shift modifications on the VDW interactions within one-dimensional cuprate materials. It introduces a combined model combining the LD and red-shift corrections, which has been labeled the LD-RS model. The research utilizes ab-initio intermolecular interaction calculations as a reference to evaluate the predicted outcomes. The findings demonstrate that the consideration of electronic-phononic red-shift corrections enhances the accuracy of VDW interaction predictions previously underestimated by the LD model. The research further identifies the red-shift corrections' sensitivity to phonon energies, demonstrating that the phonon-induced long-range electronic interactions can be substantial. The outcomes of this research will contribute to revising previous estimates of the atomic interaction energies in materials characterized by strong electron-phonon coupling, ultimately promoting a greater understanding of the atomic and molecular structures of these materials.

To ensure high-quality healthcare, it is crucial to establish a fundamental understanding of how various treatments interact. Consequently, multiple approaches have been developed to interpret and utilize existing healthcare data, including graph learning and causal reasoning. These concepts align with the principles of modular software design, where complex systems are divided into interconnected components. Inspired by this idea of modularity, we propose a novel graph learning method that mirrors the structure of software programs. We extract and analyze treatment relationships from the Minimal Hospitalization data (mphmia) to create an internal graph model. Our study focuses on building a causal network through sequential additions of nodes, aiming to create an optimal graph representation that accurately interprets the data. By applying these graph structures, we can address fundamental queries regarding treatment interactions, while also identifying unrecorded treatment combinations. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of this graph model, verifying the consistency between the constructed graph and the actual data. Additionally, through optimization, the graph model can effectively identify treatment correlations and suggest unrecorded treatment combinations, highlighting their clinical utilities.

The stability of the metastable state in chiral magnets can be explained by the presence of magnetic vortices, or skyrmions, which are stabilized by the same characteristics that make them unstable to begin with. By studying an alloy with the formula Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, researchers discovered a state where multiple skyrmions are present and then went through a process of heating and cooling to observe how the skyrmions behave under stress. Unlike other similar materials, when this alloy is subjected to pressure, it does not go through a phase shift but instead undergoes a transformation where the multiple skyrmions collapse into a single stable state. By using a variety of imaging techniques, including to neutron scattering, researchers were able to observe the transition from multiple skyrmions to a single stable state as the pressure increased. Interestingly, the alloy remains in a state of magnetic order, even under extreme pressure, which is different from other similar materials that undergo a phase shift when subjected to pressure. By using a model based on mole fraction to predict how the alloy will behave under stress, researchers found that the alloy is more resistant to pressure-induced phase shifts than other similar materials. Overall, the study provides a way to study the topological transitions in magnets by using a variety of imaging techniques and a model that predicts the behavior of magnetic vortices.

In social network analysis, a model builds a connection map of a network's evolution over time by linking an event's occurrence to the past activities within the same timeframe. This comprehensive study covers various types of high-dimensional temporal influence models, highlighting their distinct features and illustrating their utility in tackling complex problems in data mining. It also explores the practical implications of these models, prompting future researchers to explore new avenues in this field.

The concept of substantial balance within dynamic model frameworks has been extensively explored over the last twenty years, leading to the development of the method of static points, which aims to facilitate computation of Hamiltonian systems' reduced characteristic equation coefficients using static numerical models, ultimately allowing for the identification of stable and unstable periodic orbits. The method of static points, specifically applicable to balanced relative-polar action variables, has been rigorously substantiated and demonstrated to effectively address the balance problem. Building upon this foundation, we now introduce a novel approach to handling the balance problem for both static and Hamiltonian-based Variable Coordinate Transformations, which involve the use of static transformations, thereby eliminating the need for the second-order corrections term in the transfer equation, thereby simplifying the transfer equation into a first-order differential equation, similar to the Schrodinger equation. The effectiveness of this approach is illustrated by a numerical example that models a pendulum's motion.

A novel quantum steeganography algorithm based on super-dense coding is introduced, allowing for the simultaneous encoding and transmission of multiple classical bits to a single quantum bit. The proposed method uses a Bayesian neural network to determine the shared classical message, and incorporates an error correction mechanism. The feasibility of super-dense coding in steeganography is demonstrated, and the associated categorical inequality for three parties is verified. The presented scheme offers superior security and resistance to the collaborative attack of an adversary, and the probability of detection exceeds 0.95 when the adversary makes an individual attack. The accuracy of classical message recovery exceeds 0.95 when the adversary launches a collaborative attack, and the associated variance is less than 0.1.

The dynamo process in solar convective regions has been a long-standing enigma in understanding how magnetic fields are generated.
The use of mean-field frameworks has made it feasible to separate the impact of turbulence on the dynamo mechanism, however, the necessity of incorporating all related effects remains unclear.
By incorporating all relevant turbulent influences, we demonstrate that a mean-field framework with a full spectral representation is required to effectively model the dynamo process.
The computational domain encompasses the entire Sun and encompasses both the convective zone and the radiative interior.
The model successfully generates a toroidal magnetic field in the same polarity as that observed at the Sun's poles.
The efficiency of the dynamo process is found to be maximal when incorporating influences from turbulence in the barotropic and baroclinic instabilities, however, the integration of additional effects such as helicity conservation, Lorentz force feedback, and thermal flux transfer, reveals a more complex relationship.
The dynamo process becomes less efficient when certain turbulent influences are omitted, highlighting the need for a model that accounts for all relevant effects and providing insight into the potential astrophysical instabilities influencing the dynamo process.

Recent high-resolution observations at 340 GHz, made possible by the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), have revealed a massive and sudden release of molecular gas from the nucleus of the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 4945. Valued at approximately 5 x 10^6 solar masses, this catastrophic event bears striking resemblance to another massive outburst observed in another galaxy, M 82. As a result, it is suggested that the fuel supply for the extremely luminous central region in NGC 4945 is being rapidly depleted by a massive and continuous eruption of molecular gas. Furthermore, it has been proposed that the fuel supply for the central region in NGC 4945 is being regulated by an active galactic nucleus. Images at 340 GHz have effectively visualized the eruption, revealing complex structures distorted by the galaxy's rotation. In addition to the massive eruption, an extensive molecular gas disk, extending 25arcsec or 45pc or approximately 11 x 10^3 solar masses per year, has also been identified in the center of NGC 4945. As a result of the massive eruption, it is proposed that the central region in NGC 4945 is classified as an ultra-luminous infrared galaxy. Images at lower frequencies or reduced spatial resolution have effectively visualized the extensive molecular gas disk. A new numerical method for the quasilinear diffusion model has been developed to describe momentum transfer in magnetized plasmas. This model relies on a low regularity solution, consisting of a particle distribution with regularity below 1 and a regular electric potential. A Galerkin projection approach has been employed to develop the method. Due to the low regularity of the solution components, the traditional variational formulation becomes invalid, and a novel approach, termed the conservative Galerkin method, has been devised. Unlike conventional quasi-linear methods that maintain a non-conservative form, the new method adheres to a conservative form. Nonetheless, it shares a similar time discretization and maintains the maximal degree of regularity of the approximate solution components. A convergence analysis has been conducted for the new method under certain conditions. Specifically, it has been demonstrated that, for sufficiently small time steps, the error in the approximate solution remains proportional to the degree of the basis functions employed. A number of numerical tests have been performed to evaluate the new method's effectiveness. These experiments confirmed that the method can produce accurate results even with a low regularity solution. Notably, the method's accuracy is largely independent of the time step size.

The SIMSIM algorithm generates stable, exact solutions for discrete-time first- and second-order ordinary differential equations. This paper presents a variable step-size version of the SIMSIM method, known as vSDIMSIM. We investigate the convergence order of vSDIMSIM when applied to certain continuous-time problems. To make vSDIMSIM more practical, we develop a strategy for efficiently selecting the optimal step size. This approach ensures the optimal starting point by minimizing the total step count and demonstrates the convergence of the method. We also provide error estimates for vSDIMSIM when applied to certain continuous problems and extend its use to certain partial differential equations, even in cases where coefficients are missing. To facilitate the numerical computations of the vSDIMSIM method, we create a Python implementation. This implementation includes several continuous problems, discrete-time problems, and partial differential equations, along with corresponding results from the vSDIMSIM method. The results confirm the theoretical predictions regarding the accuracy of the vSDIMSIM method.

This study explores the exponential stability of abounded-c0-semigroup, specifically in the context of fixed-point theories within Banach spaces. Moreover, it investigates the relationship between Lyapunov functions and robustness. Building upon Kato's theory of semigroups of bounded-c0-semigroups in Banach spaces, our research employs a fixed-point approach to establish the exponential stability and robustness of the semigroup. By using this approach, we are able to derive necessary and sufficient conditions for exponential stability using the Lévy's robustness theorem. In addition, our research incorporates a Lyapunov function, as described in the Lévy's robustness theorem, to assess the robustness of the semigroup. In particular, we demonstrate that the semigroup's robustness is linked to the positive definiteness of a certain tensor $\mathbf A^3$ in the Lévy's robustness theorem.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational tool for determining how dimuonium interacts with substances. The code uses numerical integration, with built-in functions for substances and potential dimuonium models. It is written in Python, a language with numerous chemistry-related libraries, making it easily adaptable for studying interactions. MuMuPy is particularly suitable for educators, allowing students to model dimuonium's interaction with matter. A user manual accompanies this paper.

Investors often assess their wealth in relation to market indices or peers to gauge their financial well-being. This relative wealth perspective can serve as an alternative to the traditional risk-adjusted analysis, providing a framework to study multi-asset models. This study explores two-person models involving a risk-averse investor and a risk-neutral counterpart, with both parties holding a portfolio of assets that generate a mean-variance efficient strategy from an optimal relative wealth standpoint. We examine the scenarios where the risk-averse investor's preferences are power utilities of absolute and relative returns, optimized against a risk-free rate, and when the risk-neutral investor's objectives are aligned with the market mean and variance of returns. The latter case can be viewed as a Merton-type model for asset allocation, with the risk-neutral investor holding a multi-asset portfolio. We derive closed-form solutions for both scenarios, revealing that the risk-averse investor seeks to minimize a combination of the variance of absolute returns and a distortion factor measuring the variance of relative returns, quantifying the distinct investment needs of absolute and relative wealth management. Furthermore, we observe that the variance of relative returns contributes more significantly to the investment needs of the risk-averse investor, with the magnitude of the contribution being directly related to the distortion factor's value. This study also shows that the risk-neutral investor's investment portfolio is influenced by both the market's mean returns and the variance of returns, with the variance contributing more substantially than the mean.

Using the Hubble Space Telescope, researchers have observed the dim light of distant galaxies as they have been emitting it since the early days of the universe. Specifically, they have observed the light from galaxies that are about the size of the Milky Way or smaller, which were present in the universe when it was roughly one-sixth its current size. Initially, these galaxies were observed in the context of the discovery of Lyman-alpha break galaxies, but subsequent observations have been hindered by dust, a common substance in galaxies. It's known that dust affects observations of galaxies by absorbing or scattering light, which are further influenced by the presence of neutral gas in the galaxies. An experiment was conducted to detect this neutral gas by measuring the dim absorption of light as it passes through the galaxies' surroundings, which is due to the universe's intergalactic medium. The findings, however, suggested that dim galaxies contain less gas than they initially observed. An explanation for the discrepancy may be the presence of dim galaxies that lack prominent emission characteristics, but further research is needed to confirm these results.

We analyze the impact of quasiparticle collapse resulting from interaction with a local boson system in two models: the unitary fermionic quasiparticle box linked to a bosonic Josephson junction, and the superconducting Andreev box connected to an LC circuit. These systems can be regarded as specific realizations of the SU(2|1) symmetry protected topological scenario. In both cases, the quasiparticle collapse occurs when the bosonic circuit is in a non-degenerate ground state with nonzero bias, yielding a non-trivial SU(2) rotation, and results in a change of quasiparticle sign. Notably, this quasiparticle sign change occurs without any energy barrier involved in the process. We also investigate the impact on quasiparticle collapse due to various states of bosonic junctions: superconducting, superfluid, and insulating. Additionally, the study outlines the minimum bosonic circuit requirements to cause quasiparticle sign change, which can be realized with just one capacitor or inductance. We further explore quasiparticle sign change resulting from interaction with a single junction in the form of a quantum capacitor or Josephson junction. The study also examines quasiparticle sign change resulting from interaction with two bosonic junctions: a double Josephson junction and multiple qubit complexes. The research assesses the feasibility of observing quasiparticle collapse in various experimental systems, including spin singlet superconducting

The Thompson groups are renowned for their complex properties, and research has been carried out extensively in this area. This paper will examine the characteristics of infinite generalizations of these groups, as well as various braided versions, under a specific metric. It is demonstrated that the generalized F and R groups display distinct behavior, with the former exhibiting exponential divergence and the latter showing polynomial divergence with a degree of two, as measured by the metric established. To confirm these findings, a specific test was applied, and it is also shown that the braids have a significant impact on the metric, leading to a significant change in the divergence rate.

Recently, models like BART-Transformer and T5-Logits are being used directly in inquiry-response tasks, bypassing traditional pre-processing methods. This has led to the development of end-to-end models like RAG, which can directly query knowledge using text IDs and generate responses based on that information. This paper refines this knowledge-access approach by integrating a knowledge filter to eliminate irrelevant knowledge snippets and a response refiner to enhance the overall quality of the generated responses. The results indicate that this improved framework, BART-RAG, achieves higher response quality in terms of fact accuracy, while also demonstrating more efficient knowledge usage. The integration of a knowledge filter was implemented using the DPR seeker model. The findings suggest significant potential in using DPR as a means to selectively retrieve relevant knowledge snippets from a vast knowledge base. The implementation of this improved framework and associated code are publicly available at https://github.com/whs5503/E2E-RAG-DPR.

This study introduces a new definition for polynomials with a logarithmic burden, which comprises a particular type of polynomial, termed perpendicular, with specific properties. The investigation into these perpendicular polynomials involves examining several associated quantities, such as their zeros and the asymptotic behavior of related polynomials, which are constructed using different methods. The asymptotic behavior of these near-perpendicular and perpendicular polynomials with an arbitrary shift is described and demonstrated analytically. The orthogonality properties characteristic of orthogonal polynomials are found to be asymptotically realized under certain conditions. The analysis is supported by specific examples, which illustrate the studied phenomenon. The methods employed in this investigation draw upon the Dickson type theorem for polynomial zero distribution, the Fejér-Lotov theorem, and the principles governing the asymptotic behavior of entire functions and polynomials.

Online crowdsourcing platforms such as MTurk offer a diverse workforce with varied levels of language proficiency, making them an attractive option for evaluating automatic summarization tools. However, the task of recruiting skilled MTurk workers poses a significant challenge. Our study involves classifying workers with summarization expertise, and we achieve acceptable performance in filtering out unqualified candidates. Additionally, we assess the impact of worker experience and skill sets on summarization quality using multiple qualification criteria. Furthermore, we explore the connection between worker expertise and summarization performance across various fields. A key finding shows that expertise matters when it comes to evaluating summarization performance, and workers with relevant experience demonstrate higher quality summaries. Moreover, we observe significant variations in summarization performance depending on the worker's area of study. Interestingly, we discover that experts with a different academic background tend to produce better summaries.

Our proposed method, TS2-Net, is an innovative retrieval model for text segments that outperforms current state models, including the top-ranked model, TextVQA-RecallNet. For text retrieval, we diverge from the typical approach of merging text encodings and adopt a token-level alignment strategy based on attention. Furthermore, we introduce a token selection mechanism to improve diversity in retrieval results. Compared to existing models, TS2-Net exhibits superior performance on three benchmark datasets, achieving up to a 7.8% increase in recall rate. The development of TS2-Net involves fine-grained mining of model outputs to design effective ranking metrics and efficient hyperparameter optimization. Notably, TS2-Net's success showcases the potential of token-level operations in text retrieval, paving the way for future advancements in this area.

Beyond standard electroweak interactions, an additional neutral current exists, which also affects flavor change. Top color octonion electroweak interactions are a significant part of this process, which can also feature an analogue of the $\theta_c$ term. This $\theta_c$ term, similar to the Higgs portal $\theta_c$ term, has significant implications for high-energy interactions involving the top quark and Higgs bosons. Notably, it may cause taste-altering changes to hadronic interactions, which could be verified through experiments with lattice QCD and potentially with the LHC-b experiment by studying the $B$-meson oscillations.

A new type of random graph, known as direct hybrid hybrid random graph, is created by merging small clusters of nodes with a higher than random likelihood of connection. Researchers have conducted an in-depth study of this direct hybrid hybrid random graph. Breakthroughs have been achieved in understanding the basic structure of this graph at a larger scale, including existence and properties of the giant component and other large clusters. Findings have also shed light on the characteristics of individual clusters within the graph. Additionally, new insights have been gained into the relationship between individual nodes and the larger structure, including the characteristics of individual clusters and their shared properties. Furthermore, statistical analysis was used to confirm the consistency of the graph's structure across different node groups. Moreover, a new model has been developed to describe the relationship between early formed clusters and their shared properties. Lastly, researchers have delved into the practical applications and computational complexity aspects of the graph's structure.

The expansion of wireless communication technology has resulted in widespread interference affecting various key systems such as medical implants, navigation, railway, and aerospace equipment. To mitigate these kinds of scenes, it is crucial to identify and locate the source of wireless disturbances as swiftly as possible. Traditional approaches relying on seasoned engineers utilizing spectral analyzers are inefficient and may lead to serious consequences in emergency situations. To address this issue, this research introduces a novel real-time disturbance detection framework, encompassing a multi-label convolutional neural network model designed to automatically recognize and position wireless interference sources in diverse scenarios. To develop this real-time detection framework, this study leverages the acquisition of spectral data from actual devices and a comprehensive dataset consisting of spectral images derived from the acquisition process. By utilizing a conventional convolutional neural network, the research achieves successful single-label disturbance detection. However, due to variations in scenarios, a more advanced multi-label convolutional neural network is developed to address the challenge of identifying multiple interference sources. To validate the effectiveness of this real-time detection framework, the research demonstrates its ability to accurately detect single or multiple disturbance instances. To increase the practicality of this real-time detection framework, the research incorporates signal strength-based localization, resulting in the successful identification of disturbance instances positioned at varying signal strengths. The research finds that signal strength serves as an effective indicator of spatial consistency, facilitating the localization of disturbance sources.

This study investigates how the interactions of particles represented by a Klein-Gordon entity influence the spacetime continuum that includes a cosmic string, using the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime model as its theoretical framework. To achieve this, the formalization involves forming a nonlinear field theory as part of a larger system that includes interaction particles, a core cosmic string, and a nonlinear field. By deriving and analyzing the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of this system, the researchers are able to identify the relationships between various physical phenomena, including particle rotations, charges, and the mechanical displacement of particles. In particular, when particles acquire a degree of rotation (a property known as vorticity), the researchers observe a distinct separation of energy modes, characterized by different levels of instability, where the lower modes exhibit a significant correlation between rotation and energy, but the higher modes show a relatively less pronounced relationship. Furthermore, when particles carry an electric charge, the researchers find that the relationship between charge and energy is more complex, with regions of stability and instability overlapping with a situation known as the phonon-like domain, but the precise nature of this relationship varies significantly between rotation and mechanical displacement modes.

For any sufficiently high finite screen height, we establish that the majority of measure algebra structures, as determined by the transformation of Bernoulli shifts within the corresponding Boolean lattices, correspond to homomorphism closures of locally trivial measures. This outcome subsumes the already established result by Solel that, for high enough ranks, most measure algebras exhibit total independence.

This paper proposes a novel measurement technique for the Deep-Inelastic Scattering (DIS) target single-spin asymmetry by leveraging the recoil proton's polarization following the ep -> e p Pie+Pi- process. By adapting existing experiments that have carried out DVCS measurements, it would be feasible to undertake this novel asymmetry assessment with relatively minimal enhancements, thereby taking advantage of already-acquired data. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that this novel asymmetry is calculable via Current-Commutator methods and its production is expected to be quite small. However, testing at a high-intensity, high-precision experimental facility such as the 12 GeV Jefferson Lab or the future EIC at JLab or CEA will be essential to fully assess its utility.

Artificial intelligence's evolution is transforming, both technologically and socially. 
This progression, characterized as Enhanced Artificial Intelligence, is a theoretical model 
developing to frame and organize research in this area.  To illustrate EAI's concept, 
consider a credit Origination EAI system assessing loan applicants based not just facts but also 
environment and individual intuition, utilising algorithms interpretable only by experts. 
EAI's primary objectives include achieving measurable improvement in AI's problem-solving capacity, 
incrementally shifting decision-making authority between experts and machines, and increasing 
human trust in EAI's operations through transparent, explainable models.  This paper presents EAI's 
initialization and evaluates its practicality by applying it to a Suboptimal EAI model for decision-making.

We investigate the thermal behavior of a quantum fluid in an optical lattice, where the interaction between spin and motion causes an anisotropic superfluid, affecting the way particles move. Using a quantum Monte Carlo method, we simulated and analyzed the movement of the superfluid in the collective mode, known as the Higgs mode, along with its associated excitations. Our results show that as the system becomes more strongly linked to spin-orbit interaction, the movement of the Higgs mode becomes more uneven, and there is a significant shift in the collective mode direction at a specific temperature. These two changes occur due to the same factors that cause the movement to become uncoupled. Moreover, within a specific temperature range, the movement of the collective mode occurs at different points. These predictions are crucial for observing these collective movements in ultracold bosons in an optical lattice.

A group of vertex mappings from a graph G to itself can be classified as a degeneracy if it possesses several distinct characteristics, such as preserving the graph's structure, preserving its subgraphs, and forming a maximum group size in the graph. The most extreme form of degeneracy is a trivial group, typically denoted as Z0, which implies all vertices in the graph map to a single vertex. This article delves into various types of degeneracy, featuring a hierarchy of graph transformations where each level is characterized by a maximal group size, with the goal of identifying commonalities among these different types of graph degeneracy.

We explore the AdS/CFT connection in two and one spatial dimensions using a type IIA fibered AdS$_2$ solution, which originates from a four-dimensional AdS space. This study's primary contribution is an observation in one spatial dimension regarding a c-theorem, which serves as a form of holographic universality. The solution's simplicity in two dimensions allows for straightforward back-folding, yielding a'mirrored' geometry without additional matter fields. This process also reveals a novel black-hole geometry in one dimension, characterized by a single, negative eccentricity. The solution's simplicity provides an uncomplicated example of 'little string' in one spatial dimension, offering a potential comparison to theories with large $N$. We also explore the potential connection between our findings in two dimensions and known results within chiral theories on a string.

Our research proposes a low-noise approximation that relates Gaussian process kernels to integrated mean squared distances between functions, where we derive an expression using a fundamental mathematical operator that can incorporate various optimization techniques. By applying this to a simple linear function, we identify an optimal kernel that approximates the negative inverse Euclidean distance, a well-known kernel in mathematics. Moreover, we demonstrate the possibility of extending our framework to other functions, providing empirical justification for this approach.

This study presents an in-depth examination of strategies to minimize Mueller-scattering contributed by beam particles in muon colliders. Mueller scattering, particularly in collider machines, has been largely understudied relative to other beam-gas interactions. While design choices can significantly reduce Mueller-scattering contributions from target gas atoms, the impact from muon particle populations cannot be mitigated through design modifications. Here, the analysis of strategies to reduce Mueller-scattering contributions from muon population is conducted, considering various thermal muon population models. A potential issue with population decay rates is also addressed.

Introducing Spartan, a novel optimization technique for reducing model complexity in large neural networks, which works by selectively eliminating unnecessary neural nodes during the forward training process. The algorithm, enabled through the use of a novel, differentiable module that simulates the flow of information, treats neural weights as investments that contribute towards data prediction. The value of each neural connection is assessed and adapted continuously, similar to stock market fluctuations, leading to reduced model component redundancy. The resulting reduced models exhibit comparable performance to their original counterparts and demonstrate improved prediction efficiency, particularly on high-resolution image datasets like ImageNet. The experiments reveal intriguing parallels between neural network operation and financial market dynamics.

According to the Cayley's embedding theorem, a finite group can be incorporated into a real division ring. For instance, the Hamiltonian of a non-interacting Bose fluid embedded within a four-dimensional space corresponds to the second Pauli obstruction. This study explores whether a similar phenomenon can occur in a weakly interacting Bose fluid. We propose that the answer is yes; a superfluid Bose mixture exhibiting anisotropic interactions can represent the third Hamiltonian obstruction. This is distinct from the first obstruction that describes topological defects in the underlying symplectic group. We further support our hypothesis by identifying two distinct scenarios in which it holds true. Firstly, it can occur in mixtures featuring repulsive interactions between particles of identical mass. Secondly, it can occur in mixtures featuring attractive interactions between particles of different masses. In both scenarios, the resulting superfluid state is characterized by non-trivial spin-1 components. Specifically, the superfluid ground state exhibits a non-zero value of the spin-1 matrix $\hat{J}_z$. This is distinct from the first obstruction, as the superfluid ground state does not exhibit a non-zero value of the spin-1 matrix $\hat{J}_x$. Additionally, the superfluid ground state does not exhibit the characteristics of a spin-singlet state.

The presence of smelly code within software is widespread, causing various adverse effects that hinder project efficiency and productivity. Past research primarily focused on identifying and categorizing code smells, whereas our study delves into the opinions of software developers regarding the severity of implementation smells and their most preferred methods of remediation. Through the distribution of a survey to working professionals on a well-established platform for software developers, we collected data from over 160 participants, which enabled us to draw approximate quantitative responses regarding various coding practices and techniques related to refactoring. Our empirical analysis offers new insights that can inspire future studies on this topic, while emphasizing the necessity for developers to diligently maintain high-quality code, devoid of smelly code.

This paper investigates the resolution of variational inequalities that incorporate integro-differential terms and address situations characterized by moving constraints, even in the absence of convexity. It is demonstrated that under specified conditions, even under non-convex constraints, the values of the variational inequality can be maximized in a compact set. The findings in this context complement existing research on the sweeping action in integral systems, which is non-convex. The uses of the obtained result are considered, including a case where the motion of the constraint is also governed by a differential equation.

The fully integrated event generator, KKMCee, is now complete with the incorporation of a new photon piece that handles the initial creation of lepton and quark pairs in high-energy photon interactions. This addition builds upon the established KKMCee event generator which is utilized for electron-positron collisions. The integrated RAPCAL Monte Carlo program generates photon spectra along with KKMCee's implementation for pair production in these collisions. The resulting KKMCee includes all three components from the standalone products: the electron piece, the QED piece with polarization transfer corrections, and the RAPCAL piece handling photon spectra. The accuracy of the integrated KKMCee for pair production through photon collisions has been validated through comparisons with standalone products and PHOKAHA, another event generator that handles pair production in these interactions. The accuracy of KKMCee for the integrated cross sections, selection biases, and average hadronic energies has been confirmed in this comparison. The accuracy of KKMCee for the integrated cross sections, average selection biases, and average energies of hadronic interactions for pair production has been confirmed to be within one percent. The accuracy of KKMCee for the integrated energies of hadronic interactions for pair production has been confirmed to be within the range of 0.01 to 0.1 percent.
